Ingredient Substitutions

1 egg = ¼ cup applesauce or 1 tbsp ground flax + 3 tbsp water. ¾ cup honey replaces 1 cup sugar. 3 tbsp cocoa + 1 tbsp butter replaces 1 oz unsweetened chocolate. 1 tsp table salt = 1¼ tsp Morton kosher = about 2¼ tsp Diamond Crystal.

The four swaps at a glance
Out ofUseWatch out for
1 egg¼ cup applesauce, ¼ cup mashed banana, or 1 tbsp ground flax + 3 tbsp waterNot for meringues or custards
1 cup sugar¾ cup honey, and cut other liquid by 3 tbspAdd a little baking soda; bake 25 °F lower

Egg substitutes

One egg = ¼ cup unsweetened applesauce, ¼ cup mashed ripe banana, or 1 tablespoon ground flaxseed stirred into 3 tablespoons water and left 5 minutes to thicken.

—

Best for: muffins, pancakes, quick breads and brownies. Not good for: meringues, custards, soufflés or anything where eggs are the main ingredient.

Honey for sugar (and back)

Use ¾ cup honey for each cup of sugar. Honey is about 17% water, so for each cup of honey you use, cut the other liquid by ¼ cup, add ½ teaspoon baking soda to balance its acidity, and bake 25 °F lower so it doesn’t brown too fast. Those adjustments follow the National Honey Board’s baking tips.

Direction

—

Best for: quick breads, muffins, granola and cakes that should stay moist. Not good for: crisp cookies, or recipes that cream butter and sugar for lift.

Cocoa powder for unsweetened chocolate

For each ounce of unsweetened baking chocolate, use 3 tablespoons natural cocoa powder plus 1 tablespoon melted butter or oil. Natural and Dutch-process cocoa aren’t interchangeable in recipes that rely on baking soda, because only natural cocoa is acidic enough to react with it.

—

Best for: brownies, cakes and frostings. Not good for: dipping, ganache or anything where the chocolate needs to set firm.

Table salt and kosher salt

A teaspoon of table salt weighs about 6 g. Kosher salt crystals are bigger and hollower, so a teaspoon holds less: Morton kosher about 4.8 g, Diamond Crystal about 2.7 g. That’s why 1 tsp table salt equals 1¼ tsp Morton kosher but about 2¼ tsp Diamond Crystal.

—

Salt by volume, same saltiness
Table saltMorton kosherDiamond CrystalWeight
1 tsp table salt1¼ tsp2¼ tsp6 g
2 tsp table salt2½ tsp4½ tsp12 g
3 tsp table salt3¾ tsp6¾ tsp18 g

Best for: cooking, seasoning and most baking. Not good for: bread dough, brines and cures, where a small error matters; weigh the salt in grams for those.

Weights from Morton’s conversion chart (1 tsp table = 1¼ tsp kosher) and King Arthur’s ingredient weight chart (table salt 18 g and Diamond Crystal 8 g per tablespoon). Volume is approximate because crystal size varies; weigh salt in grams when it matters.

How it works

Each calculator multiplies your amount by the swap above and rounds to amounts you can measure. It all runs in your browser. Nothing you type is sent anywhere or saved.

Ways to use it

  • Out of eggs. Applesauce or flax gets muffins and pancakes done.
  • Honey and sugar. Swap honey in for sugar, or sugar in when a recipe calls for honey and you’re out.
  • A recipe calls for unsweetened chocolate. Cocoa and butter from the pantry do the job.
  • A different salt. Converting a recipe written for Diamond Crystal to table salt, or the other way.

Questions

Can I replace eggs in any recipe?

No. Swaps work when eggs are there for moisture and binding, as in muffins, pancakes and quick breads. They don’t work when eggs are the structure, as in meringues, custards, soufflés and angel food cake.

Does honey make things sweeter than sugar?

Yes, cup for cup honey is sweeter, which is why ¾ cup replaces a full cup of sugar. It also browns faster and keeps baked goods moister.

Can I swap natural and Dutch cocoa?

Not in recipes that use baking soda. Natural cocoa is acidic and reacts with baking soda to make the cake rise; Dutch-process cocoa has been treated to remove that acidity. Recipes with baking powder are more forgiving.

Why does kosher salt measure differently?

The crystals are bigger and pack loosely, so a spoonful holds less salt. Diamond Crystal is especially light: you need about 2¼ teaspoons to match 1 teaspoon of table salt. Morton kosher is denser, at 1¼ teaspoons.

Is anything saved?

No. The calculators run in your browser and nothing is saved or sent anywhere.
